title: The Doorman

post.author: u/night_audit_nell
post.title: I'm the night auditor at an old hotel. For over four hours, our check-in kiosks told one guest in four that Room 13 wasn't answering. Nobody has stayed in Room 13 since 1974.

blocks.text: I'm the night auditor at the Vesper Hotel: 96 rooms, a brass revolving door and, after midnight, just me at the desk. Late guests check themselves in at two kiosks in the lobby. The kiosks, our booking website and the key-card machine all run on four small servers in the old luggage room.

Cas, the contractor who set them up in 2019, named them after the four rooms on our first floor: room-11, room-12, room-13 and room-14. In front of them sits a fifth machine he calls the Doorman. It's a load balancer: it sends each request to the next room in turn, 11, 12, 13, 14, then 11 again. Cas calls that round robin. At night about 48 requests arrive each second, so each room gets 12, and each can finish 20.
Early on Sunday a woman came to the desk holding a slip from kiosk 2. The kiosk had spun for ten seconds, then printed this:

She had booked a double on the third floor. Room 13 is real. It's on the first floor, it has been locked since 1974, and its key hangs behind me on a hook nobody touches. By 3 AM nine guests had come to the desk with the same slip. Every one of them had pressed retry and got in the second time.
Cas's dashboard, which I can read but not change, said the same thing all night:

01:47:12  room-13   last answer
01:47:22  doorman   request to room-13: no answer in 10 s (timeout)
02:15:00  arriving 48/s   served 36/s   failed 12/s   p95 625 ms
02:15:00  room-11 12/s   room-12 12/s   room-13 12/s   room-14 12/s
05:58:41  doorman   request to room-13: no answer in 10 s (timeout)

Cas came in at six. Room-13's machine had frozen at 1:47 and answered nothing after that. The Doorman never knew. It never asks a room whether anyone is in. It just kept sending every fourth guest to a door that wouldn't open. The slips name the room, Cas says, so he can tell which one failed.
The Doorman has worked every night since 2019. It has never once knocked.
He restarted room-13 at 6:10 and it came back. Then he asked me to post this, because the Doorman is one machine too, and he no longer trusts it. What should he change before next weekend?

blocks.label: doorman_dashboard_0215.png

diagram.aria: Cas's dashboard at 2:15 AM on Sunday. 48 requests a second from guests reach the Doorman, a load balancer that hands them out in turn and never checks a room. It sends 12 a second to each of room-11, room-12, room-13 and room-14. Rooms 11, 12 and 14 answer theirs and are 60% busy. Room-13 has not answered since 1:47, so each of its 12 requests a second waits 10 seconds and fails.

blocks.caption: Cas redrew his dashboard from 2:15 AM for me. 48 requests a second reach the Doorman, which hands them out in turn, 12 to each room. Rooms 11, 12 and 14 answer theirs and are 60% busy. Room 13 hasn't answered since 1:47, but it still gets its 12 a second, and every one of them waits ten seconds and fails.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your Doorman has a list and a turn order, and nothing else. A load balancer can learn that a room is gone in two ways. An active health check: every few seconds it asks each room a small question, usually GET /health, and expects 200 OK back. How often it asks is the interval. The threshold is how many misses in a row before it stops sending guests to that room, and how many answers in a row before it lets the room back in. A passive check watches real requests fail instead. Now the arithmetic: if it asks every 10 seconds and gives up after 3 misses, how long can a frozen room keep swallowing guests? And at 12 a second, how many guests is that?

replies.author: u/night_audit_nell
replies.text: Cas says at most 30 seconds. He did the second sum on a napkin and folded it before I could read it.

comments.author: u/late_checkout_lou
comments.text: Ask Cas whether all four rooms run at the same speed. Round robin assumes they do. Least connections sends each new request to the room with the fewest requests still in progress, so a slow room, which stays busy longer, gets fewer. Weighted round robin does it by hand: each room gets a weight, and a room with weight 2 gets twice the share of a room with weight 1.

replies.author: u/night_audit_nell
replies.text: They don't, on Wednesdays. The weekly backup runs on room-14 from 2 to 4 AM, and while it runs that room finishes about 4 requests a second instead of 20. Cas says guests who land there wait about ten seconds, and once its line of 40 is full, the rest get a 503.

comments.author: u/two_am_deploy
comments.text: Once Cas has checks, he'll also take rooms out on purpose, for updates. Don't just switch one off: every request it's halfway through dies with it. Drain it first. Tell the load balancer to stop sending it new requests, let the ones already inside finish, then remove it. That's connection draining. Most load balancers let you set the longest they'll wait, often called the deregistration delay.

comments.author: u/revolving_door_rhys
comments.text: Cas is right to worry about the Doorman itself. One machine in front of four is your new single point of failure: if it stops, the rooms are fine and nobody can reach them. Run two. One works and one stands by, and they share one address, so when the first stops answering, the standby takes the address over within seconds. Or rent a managed load balancer, which the cloud company runs as several machines in different zones for you.

reply.prompt: Cas has until next weekend. What should he change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add a fifth room. If one room stops answering, the other four can carry the night, and only one guest in five is affected instead of one in four.
options.part2: Cas added room-15 on Thursday. On Sunday at 2:41 AM room-12 froze. The Doorman kept sending it every fifth request, about 10 a second, until Cas came in at six. Eleven guests came to the desk with slips that said ROOM 12 IS NOT ANSWERING. The other four rooms were barely busy. Nobody had asked whether any of them were alive either. They just were.
options.senior: More servers make each failure a smaller slice, but they don't make the load balancer notice. Without a health check, a dead server keeps its full share until a person removes it, however many healthy ones stand beside it.

options.text: Turn on health checks: the Doorman asks every room GET /health every 10 seconds, takes a room out after 3 misses in a row and lets it back in after 3 answers. Switch to least connections, drain a room before taking it out on purpose, and run the Doorman as a pair that shares one address.
options.part2: Cas set it up on Thursday, with a second Doorman standing by. On Sunday at 2:41:05 AM room-12 froze. The Doorman asked it at 2:41:10, :20 and :30, heard nothing three times, and took it out at 2:41:30, 25 seconds after it froze. In those 25 seconds about 300 requests failed and one guest came to the desk. Then the other three rooms took 16 a second each, 80% busy with a p95 of 1,250 ms, and nobody else noticed. Cas restarted room-12 at 3:05; it answered three checks in a row and was back before 3:06. On Wednesday least connections gave the backup room about 3 requests a second instead of 12, and nobody got a 503. On Saturday he drained room-11 for an update: the 8 requests it was in the middle of finished, and not one failed. He took the room names off the slips, too. Last night at 4:10 the standby Doorman took over the address for two seconds, then gave it back. Cas checked. Neither machine had restarted.
options.senior: A load balancer is only as good as its list. Health checks keep the list honest within a time you chose, at most the interval times the threshold, here 30 seconds. Least connections steers guests away from a slow room, draining makes planned removals free, and two doormen sharing one address mean the front door isn't the next single point of failure.

options.text: Keep the Doorman as it is, but make the kiosks and the website retry: if a room doesn't answer within 10 seconds, send the same request again. The guests who pressed retry all got in.
options.part2: Cas added automatic retries. On Sunday at 2:41 AM room-12 froze. No slips came out of the kiosks. Instead, every fourth guest watched a spinner for ten seconds before the retry went to the next room and worked. The Doorman still sent room-12 its 12 requests a second until six. At 2:52 a guest came to the desk with two receipts: room-12 had charged her card just before it froze, and the retry charged it again.
options.senior: Retrying on another server is a real tool, and it's what a passive health check builds on. On its own it hides the dead room instead of removing it: every guest who lands there still waits out the full timeout, and a retried POST can run twice unless it's idempotent.

options.text: Set up an alert that wakes Cas when a room stops answering, so he can take it out of the Doorman's list by hand within minutes.
options.verdict: Trade-off: someone has to wake up
options.part2: Cas set up the alert. On Sunday at 2:41 AM room-12 froze, and his phone rang at 2:42. He woke on the third call, logged in at 2:59 and took room-12 out of the list at 3:01. Twenty minutes at 12 failed requests a second is about 14,000 failed requests, and eleven guests at the desk. On Wednesday the alert never rang at all. Room-14 was answering, just slowly, and round robin kept giving it a quarter of the guests.
options.senior: Alerts are for people and health checks are for machines. A person takes minutes, and at 3 AM often many; a load balancer takes seconds. Keep the alert so someone fixes the room, but let the load balancer steer around it first.

sim.title: Run the Doorman
sim.lede: You're Cas, replaying Sunday night at the Vesper. The dots are a sample of the requests guests send, and the numbers count all of them, per second. Each room can finish 20 requests a second, and room-14 only 4 while the Wednesday backup runs. Past that, requests wait in the room's line, which holds 40, and when it's full they get 503. A room that stops answering makes every request sent to it wait 10 seconds, then fail. The p95 wait is a teaching model: an idle room answers in 250 ms, and the wait climbs as a room fills up. Least connections is modeled by where it settles: each room's share follows how fast it finishes requests. To keep it simple, one threshold sets both the misses that take a room out and the answers that bring it back. The clock runs 5 times faster than real life. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: with health checks off and room 13 picked, press Room stops answering. 12 requests a second fail and room-13 keeps a quarter of the share, as on Sunday. Reset, turn health checks on (every 10 seconds, 3 in a row) and stop room 13 again: the time to detect is never more than 30 seconds, and the failed total stops climbing. Revive it and count three answers before it's back. Then turn on the Wednesday backup under round robin, and switch to least connections. Try weighted round robin with 2:1:1:1. Last, drain and remove one room, then stop another, and compare the failed total.

explain.oneLine: Nothing haunted Room 13. A server froze, and the load balancer in front of it never checked whether its servers were alive, so for over four hours it kept sending a quarter of all requests to a machine that couldn't answer.

steps.title: A load balancer is a doorman with a list.
steps.text: Clients never pick a server. They connect to one address, the load balancer's, and it chooses a server from its list for each new connection or request, passes the request on and carries the answer back. That's what lets you add, remove or replace servers without telling anyone. Load balancers come in two kinds, named after layers of the OSI model, a standard way to describe a network as seven layers. A layer 4 (L4) load balancer works at the transport layer. It sees TCP connections, addresses and ports, picks a server once per connection and passes the bytes through without reading them: fast, and fine for any protocol. A layer 7 (L7) load balancer works at the application layer. It reads each HTTP request, so it can send /api to one set of servers and /images to another, look at headers and cookies, choose a server per request and check health with a real request. To read HTTPS it has to decrypt it, so it holds the certificate and does more work per request. The Doorman is L7: it hands out requests, not connections.

steps.title: How it chooses: four algorithms.
steps.text: Round robin hands requests out in turn. It's simple and even, and right when servers are alike and requests cost about the same. Weighted round robin gives each server a weight and a share to match: weights 2, 1, 1 and 1 send 40% to the first server and 20% to each of the others. Use it when servers differ in a way you know in advance, like one bigger machine. Least connections sends each new request to the server with the fewest requests in progress. A slow server stays busy longer, so it's picked more rarely, and nobody has to set anything: on Wednesday it would have given the backup room 3 requests a second instead of 12, and the other rooms 15 each. On AWS the same idea is called least outstanding requests. At large scale there's a catch: many load balancers each see only their own counts, and comparing every server for every request takes time. Random with two choices picks two servers at random and sends the request to the one with fewer in progress. It sounds lazy, but it gets most of the benefit.

steps.title: Health checks: knocking on every door.
steps.text: In the last case, Nils had to take a dead server out of the list by hand. A load balancer without health checks does exactly that: it keeps a dead server's full share until a person removes it, which here meant 12 requests a second for over four hours. An active health check asks every server a small question on a timer, usually GET /health, and counts the answers. Enough misses in a row, the unhealthy threshold, and the server is out of service; enough answers in a row, the healthy threshold, and it's back. The worst case is easy to work out. If a server dies just after a check, the first miss comes a full interval later, so it's out at most the interval times the threshold later: 10 seconds times 3 is 30. If it dies just before a check, it's out after 20. A server that hangs instead of refusing adds the check's timeout to each miss. Until then its share keeps failing, so detection has a price: about 12 a second for 25 seconds is 300 requests. A passive health check learns from real traffic instead: by default nginx marks a server unavailable for 10 seconds after one failed request. Shorter intervals and lower thresholds notice sooner, but they also throw out a server that was only slow for a moment, let it back, and throw it out again.

steps.title: Taking a server out on purpose: drain it first.
steps.text: Switching a server off cuts every request it's in the middle of. Draining takes it out gently: the load balancer stops sending it new requests, waits for the ones in progress to finish, and only then takes it off the list, after which the server can stop with a graceful shutdown. At the Vesper a room at 12 requests a second has about 8 in progress, each answered within a second or so, so a drain takes almost no time. The wait has a ceiling, the deregistration delay, for requests and connections that run long, like a big upload or a WebSocket, and whatever is still running when it ends is cut. Draining is for removals you plan, like an update or scaling in. A crash gives no warning, which is why you need health checks as well.

steps.title: The doorman can be the single point of failure.
steps.text: Put one load balancer in front of four servers and you've moved the single point of failure to the front door: if it stops, every server is fine and nobody can reach them. There are two usual answers. A pair: two load balancers, one active and one standing by, share a virtual IP address, an address that can move between machines. They exchange heartbeats, and if the active one goes quiet, the standby claims the address within seconds. Or a managed load balancer: the cloud company runs it as several machines, at least one in each availability zone you enable, replaces them when they fail and adds more as traffic grows, and clients find them through DNS. Either way it's still one shared part. A bad configuration change, or a fault in the service that manages it, reaches every server behind it at once.

diagram.aria: The fix, at 2:41:30 AM the next Sunday. Guests reach one address, held by Doorman A, the active load balancer. Doorman B stands by and watches it, ready to take the address over. Doorman A uses least connections and health checks every 10 seconds. Room-12 froze and missed 3 checks in a row, so it is out: it still gets GET /health checks but no guests. Rooms 11, 13 and 14 get 16 requests a second each and are 80% busy.

notes.text: GET /health every 10 s: out after 3 misses, back after 3 answers

explain.caption: The fix, drawn at 2:41:30 on the next Sunday. Doorman A holds the hotel's one address, and Doorman B watches it, ready to take the address over. Room-12 froze and missed three checks in a row, so A has taken it out: it still asks it GET /health every 10 seconds, but sends it no guests. The other three rooms take 16 requests a second each, 80% busy. When room-12 answers three checks in a row, it goes back in.

fix.title: The fix: check every door, choose by load, drain before removing, and never one doorman
fix.text: Turn on active health checks against a cheap /health that proves the server itself can answer: every 10 seconds, out after 3 misses in a row, back after 3 answers. Work out the cost before choosing the numbers: at most 30 seconds to notice, with the dead server's share failing until then. Pick the algorithm for the servers you actually have: round robin when they're alike, least connections when speeds or request costs vary, weights when you know the difference in advance. Drain before every planned removal, with a deregistration delay longer than your slowest normal request. Run the load balancer as a pair sharing one address, or use a managed one across at least two availability zones. Keep the alert as well, so a person repairs what the load balancer steers around. And take server names off public error pages: guests don't need them, and attackers like a map.

limits: A health check only knows what it asks. A /health that answers 200 OK while the server can't reach its database passes, and guests still fail. Make it ask about every dependency instead, and one slow database fails every server's check at once, so the load balancer throws out all of them. AWS's Application Load Balancer fails open when that happens, sending traffic to every target anyway, but a simpler load balancer like the Doorman may serve nobody.

Detection is never instant, and the dead server's share fails until the last missed check. A server that answers errors in a millisecond instead of hanging is worse for least connections: it always looks idle, so it attracts more requests, not fewer. Only the health check takes it off the list.

Moving requests between servers assumes any server can answer any request. If a guest's sign-in lives in one server's memory, a request sent to another server forgets them, and draining or ejecting that server signs everyone on it out. That's the next case.

explain.seniorTake: Name both choices, with numbers. The algorithm decides who gets the next request; the health check decides who's on the list, and the list matters more: round robin over healthy servers beats the cleverest algorithm over a list with a dead server on it. Use round robin when servers and requests are alike and least connections when they aren't. Choose the interval and threshold on purpose, multiply them to get the worst-case time to notice, and multiply again by the dead server's share to know what it costs. Keep /health honest but shallow, drain before every planned removal, and make sure the load balancer itself is at least two of something.

realWorld.title: How an AWS Application Load Balancer checks its targets
realWorld.text: AWS calls the servers behind its load balancers targets. For EC2 instance and IP targets, an Application Load Balancer sends each one a health check every 30 seconds by default (the interval can be 5 to 300 seconds), and a check with no answer within 5 seconds, the default timeout, fails. After 2 failures in a row, the default unhealthy threshold, it takes the target out of service; after 5 successes in a row, the default healthy threshold, it puts the target back. So with the defaults, a frozen target can keep its share for up to about a minute, and a recovered one waits about two and a half minutes to return. Each load balancer node checks every target itself. If every target fails its checks at the same time, the load balancer fails open and sends traffic to all of them anyway.

realWorld.title: Algorithms and draining on an Application Load Balancer
realWorld.text: Round robin is the default routing algorithm for an Application Load Balancer's targets. Least outstanding requests, which picks the target with the fewest requests in progress, and weighted random are the alternatives, one at a time. When you deregister a target, it enters the draining state: the load balancer stops sending it new requests and waits for the deregistration delay, 300 seconds by default, so requests already in progress can finish. If the target has no requests in progress and no open connections, deregistration completes at once. If the target closes a connection before the delay is over, the client gets a 500-level error.

realWorld.title: An Application Load Balancer reads requests
realWorld.text: AWS's Application Load Balancer works at the application layer, the seventh layer of the OSI model. Its listener rules can send requests to different targets by the path in the URL, the hostname, HTTP headers and methods, query parameters or source IP addresses, so one load balancer can sit in front of several services, each with its own health checks.

realWorld.title: A Network Load Balancer reads connections
realWorld.text: AWS's Network Load Balancer works at the fourth layer of the OSI model and, AWS says, can handle millions of requests per second. It doesn't read requests. For TCP it picks a target with a flow hash of the protocol, the source and destination IP addresses and ports, and the TCP sequence number, and keeps each connection on that one target for the life of the connection. A client's separate connections can land on different targets.

realWorld.title: A managed load balancer is many machines
realWorld.text: When you enable an availability zone for an AWS load balancer, Elastic Load Balancing creates a load balancer node in that zone, and an Application Load Balancer must have at least two zones enabled. Clients find the nodes through DNS: Amazon's DNS servers return the nodes' IP addresses with a TTL of 60 seconds, so the addresses can change quickly, and Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer as traffic changes.

realWorld.title: nginx: weights, least connections and passive checks
realWorld.text: nginx is a widely used web server that is often run as a load balancer. By default it spreads requests over the servers in an upstream block with weighted round robin: with weights 5, 1 and 1, every 7 requests go 5 to the first server and one to each of the others. Its least_conn method picks the server with the fewest active connections, taking weights into account, and random two picks two servers at random and then the one with fewer active connections. The free version checks passively: by default, one failed attempt within 10 seconds (max_fails=1, fail_timeout=10s) marks a server unavailable for 10 seconds. Periodic active health checks are part of its commercial subscription.

realWorld.title: The power of two random choices
realWorld.text: In 2001 Michael Mitzenmacher published an analysis of what he called the supermarket model in IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems: customers arrive at n servers, and each one picks d servers at random and waits at the one with the fewest customers. He found that d = 2 choices gives an exponential improvement over d = 1 in the expected time a customer spends in the system, while d = 3 is only a constant factor better than d = 2. It's the idea behind random-with-two-choices methods like nginx's random two.

realWorld.title: When the managed load balancer breaks: AWS, December 24, 2012
realWorld.text: AWS's own summary describes a maintenance process that was run against the production ELB state data by mistake at 12:24 PM PST on December 24, 2012, in the US-East Region, deleting a portion of the ELB state data. Running load balancers kept handling requests at first, but the ones the control plane then changed were set up wrongly, and at the peak 6.8% of running ELB load balancers were affected, with errors and degraded performance for customers' applications. The service was back to normal at 12:05 PM PST on December 25. AWS then changed access to that data so that changes need specific change management approval. Many machines remove the single box, not every shared failure.

asked: Where does the load balancer sit in your URL shortener, and what happens when one of the redirect servers dies?
Round robin or least connections? How quickly does your load balancer notice a dead server, and what does that cost?
interview.answer: Draw it in one line. Clients find the service through DNS and reach a load balancer that is itself redundant, a pair or a managed one across at least two availability zones. It spreads requests over identical redirect servers, which look up short codes in a shared store. Make it L7: it holds the certificate for HTTPS and can send /api, where new links are created, to a different set of servers than the redirects. Then name the choices with numbers. Redirects are small and alike, so round robin is fine, or least connections if some requests, like creating links, cost much more. Active health checks on a shallow /health every 10 seconds, out after 2 or 3 misses: a dead server is noticed within 20 to 30 seconds, and with ten servers, a tenth of requests fail until then. Redirects are GETs, so they can be retried safely on another server. Drain servers on every deploy. Then say what limits you next: the shared store, which later cases this season cover.

terms.def: The hotel worker who runs the front desk overnight and checks the day's accounts. At the Vesper, the only person awake when the kiosks fail.
A screen in a hotel lobby where guests check themselves in and get a key card without going to the desk.
The machine at a hotel that writes a room's code onto a plastic key card at check-in.
Cas's name for the Vesper's load balancer, because it greets every request and sends it to a room.
The turning circle a screen shows while it waits for an answer.
Running but not answering anything. A frozen server holds every request until the caller's timeout runs out, which is harder to spot than a server that's switched off.
To stop responding without closing the connection, so the caller waits until its timeout. Room-13's machine hung at 1:47.
The rule a load balancer uses to choose a server for each request or connection, such as round robin or least connections. AWS calls it the routing algorithm.
Handing requests to servers in turn: first, second, third, fourth, then first again. Even and simple, but blind to how busy each server is.
A number given to a server that sets its share. With weights 2, 1, 1 and 1, the first server gets 2 of every 5 requests.
Round robin where each server's share matches its weight. With weights 5, 1 and 1, nginx sends 5 of every 7 requests to the first server.
Said of a request a server has received but not answered yet. Also called in-flight or outstanding.
Sending each new request to the server with the fewest requests or connections in progress. A slow server stays busy longer, so it gets fewer.
AWS's name for least connections on an Application Load Balancer: each request goes to the target with the fewest requests in progress.
An Application Load Balancer algorithm that sends requests evenly across healthy targets in random order, and can send fewer to a target with many more errors than the rest.
Pick two servers at random and send the request to the one with fewer in progress. Nearly as good as least connections, and cheaper when there are many load balancers.
The finding that letting each arrival pick the less busy of two random servers, instead of one, makes waits dramatically shorter.
A health check the load balancer sends on a timer, such as GET /health every 10 seconds, whether or not any guests are arriving.
Judging a server's health from real traffic: when requests to it fail, the load balancer stops using it for a while. nginx's free version works this way.
A path many services answer just for health checks, usually with 200 OK and a few bytes. Also called a health check endpoint.
How often a load balancer runs a health check against each server: 10 seconds in Cas's fix, 30 seconds by default on an AWS Application Load Balancer.
How many health checks in a row it takes to change a server's state. The sim uses one threshold for both directions; real load balancers set two.
How many failed health checks in a row take a server out of service. 2 by default on an AWS Application Load Balancer.
How many passed health checks in a row bring a server back into service. 5 by default on an AWS Application Load Balancer.
How long a load balancer waits for an answer to a health check before counting it as a miss. 5 seconds by default on an AWS Application Load Balancer.
On the load balancer's list of servers that get new requests. A server taken out of rotation gets none, though it may still be checked.
Taken off the list of servers that get requests after failing health checks. The load balancer keeps checking it and puts it back when it answers again.
How long between a server failing and the load balancer taking it out: at most the interval times the unhealthy threshold, plus timeouts if the server hangs.
Taking a server out gently: stop sending it new requests, let the ones in progress finish, then remove it. Also called draining.
To take a server out of a load balancer with connection draining.
The longest a load balancer waits for a draining server's requests to finish before removing it anyway. 300 seconds by default on AWS.
To add a server to a load balancer's list. To deregister is to remove it.
To remove a server from a load balancer's list. On AWS the server is drained first.
AWS's word for a server, container or IP address that a load balancer sends requests to.
On AWS, a list of targets with its own health check settings, routing algorithm and deregistration delay. A listener rule sends requests to one.
The part of a load balancer that waits for connections on one port and protocol, such as HTTPS on port 443.
An if-then rule on an Application Load Balancer listener, such as: if the path starts with /api, send the request to this target group.
Open Systems Interconnection model: a standard way to describe a network in seven layers, from cables at layer 1 to applications such as HTTP at layer 7.
Layer 4 of the OSI model, where TCP and UDP carry data between programs, identified by addresses and ports.
Layer 7 of the OSI model, where protocols such as HTTP carry requests and responses that programs understand.
Working at the transport layer. An L4 load balancer sees connections, addresses and ports, not requests, and sends a whole connection to one server.
Working at the application layer. An L7 load balancer reads each request, its path, headers and cookies, and can choose a server per request.
AWS's load balancing service. It includes the Application Load Balancer (layer 7) and the Network Load Balancer (layer 4).
Short for Elastic Load Balancing, AWS's load balancing service, or one load balancer it runs.
AWS's layer 4 load balancer. It keeps each TCP connection on one target for the connection's life and can handle millions of requests per second.
A way to pick a server from the details of a connection, such as its protocol, addresses, ports and sequence number, so the whole connection goes to the same server.
One of the machines that together make up a managed load balancer. AWS creates one in each availability zone you enable.
What some load balancers do when every server fails its health checks: send traffic to all of them anyway, on the bet that the checks are wrong.
An IP address that isn't tied to one machine and can move to another, so clients keep using the same address when the machine behind it changes.
Two load balancers sharing a virtual IP address: one handles the traffic, the other watches its heartbeats and takes the address over if it goes quiet.
A load balancer a cloud company runs for you as several machines across zones, replacing failed ones and adding more as traffic grows.
A copy of data made in case the original is lost. Making one reads a lot of data, which slows the server it runs on.
Something a service needs in order to work, such as a database or a payment service.
A health check that tests only the server itself: the program is running and can answer. It can't fail because something else is slow.
A health check that also tests what the server depends on, such as its database. More honest, but one shared problem fails every server's check at once.
A connection that starts as an HTTP request and then stays open, so both sides can send messages at any time. Common for chat and live updates.
The IP address a request or connection comes from.
A widely used free web server, often run as a load balancer in front of other servers. A paid version adds more features.
In nginx, the set of servers it passes requests to, written as an upstream block with one server line each.
nginx's passive health check settings: after max_fails failed attempts within fail_timeout, a server is skipped for fail_timeout. The defaults are 1 and 10 seconds.
A paid version of a product with extra features. nginx's adds periodic active health checks.
A computer scientist at Harvard University who published the 2001 analysis of the power of two random choices in load balancing.
Mitzenmacher's model of load balancing: customers arrive at many servers, and each picks a few servers at random and joins the shortest line among them.
An improvement that grows like repeated multiplication, not addition. Here: waits shrink far more than twice when going from one random choice to two.
Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, a professional body that publishes research journals such as IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems.
The live system that real customers use, as opposed to test copies.
The part of a service that changes its setup, such as creating or reconfiguring load balancers. The data plane is the part that carries the actual traffic.
The part of a service that carries the actual traffic, such as a running load balancer passing requests to servers.
The records AWS keeps about every load balancer's configuration and the servers behind it, which its control plane uses to manage them.
A process where changes to production systems need review and approval before anyone makes them.
AWS's region in northern Virginia, also called us-east-1.
A CloudWatch metric for an AWS load balancer: how many of a target group's targets are passing their health checks.

atWork: Open the EC2 console for your team's production account (read-only access is enough), go to Target Groups and pick the one in front of a service you know. On the Health checks tab, read the protocol, the path, the interval, the timeout and both thresholds. Multiply the interval by the unhealthy threshold: that's how long a dead target can keep its share. Multiply it by the healthy threshold: that's how long a fixed one waits to come back. Then ask what the path actually tests, only the server or everything behind it. On the Attributes tab, read the load balancing algorithm and the deregistration delay, and compare the delay with your slowest normal request. On the Targets tab, check each target's health status and look for any that are draining or unhealthy. Last, open the load balancer itself, count the availability zones it's enabled in, and look at its HealthyHostCount in CloudWatch for the last week: any dips nobody mentioned?

recall.prompt: Your API runs on 6 EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer with the default health checks: every 30 seconds, out after 2 failures in a row. At 3 PM one instance freezes while 600 requests a second arrive. Roughly how long until the load balancer stops sending it requests, how many requests fail meanwhile, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Up to about a minute: the interval times the unhealthy threshold, 30 s times 2
Its share fails until then: about 100 a second, up to about 6,000 requests
Notice sooner with a shorter interval or lower threshold, accepting more false alarms
Retry idempotent requests on another instance, and alert a person to fix the frozen one

recall.model: Up to about a minute. With a 30-second interval and an unhealthy threshold of 2, the frozen instance is taken out between 30 and 60 seconds after it freezes, plus up to the 5-second timeout on each check because it hangs instead of refusing. Until then it keeps a sixth of the traffic, about 100 requests a second, so up to roughly 6,000 requests fail. I'd shorten that, for example a 10-second interval with a threshold of 2, which notices within 20 seconds at the cost of more checks and a bit more risk of throwing out an instance that was only slow for a moment. I'd make sure /health tests the instance itself, let clients or the load balancer retry idempotent requests on another instance, and keep an alert so a person fixes the frozen one.

recall.prompt: Four servers sit behind round robin. On Wednesday nights one of them runs a backup and finishes a fifth as many requests as the others. Which algorithm sends it fewer requests without anyone changing a setting?
options: Weighted round robin with equal weights
None: every algorithm gives it a quarter
recall.why: Least connections sends each new request to the server with the fewest in progress. The slow server stays busy longer, so it's picked more rarely, and it adapts the moment the backup starts or stops. Weights would work too, but only if someone sets them every Wednesday.

recall.prompt: You want requests for /api to go to one set of servers and requests for /images to another, all behind one address. What do you need?
options: A layer 4 load balancer, because it's faster
A layer 7 load balancer, because it reads each request's path
Health checks on both sets of servers
recall.why: Only a layer 7 load balancer reads the HTTP request, so only it can see the path. A layer 4 one sees connections, addresses and ports, and passes the bytes through unread.

recall.prompt: At 2 PM you need to patch one of four servers behind a load balancer. A teammate says: just stop it, the health checks will take it out within 30 seconds. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: Stopping it cuts the requests in progress, and its share fails until the checks notice
Drain it first: deregister it so it gets nothing new, and let current requests finish
Then stop it gracefully, and add it back once it passes its health checks
Check the other three can carry its share

recall.model: Not like that. Health checks are for failures you didn't plan. If you just stop it, every request it's working on is cut, and for up to 30 seconds the load balancer keeps sending it a quarter of the traffic, which all fails. Drain it instead: deregister it so the load balancer sends it nothing new, wait for the requests in progress to finish, which the deregistration delay caps, then stop it with a graceful shutdown. First check the other three can carry its share at 2 PM. After patching, register it again and let it pass its health checks before it takes traffic.

recall.prompt: Cas has health checks on all four rooms, but the Doorman is still one machine. At 4 AM its power supply fails. What happens, and what's the usual fix?
options: The rooms notice and take requests directly
The health checks move traffic to a healthy room
Nothing reaches any room until the Doorman is back: run a pair sharing one address, or a managed load balancer
DNS sends guests to the rooms instead
recall.why: Health checks protect against a dead server behind the load balancer, not against the load balancer itself. One machine in front of everything is a single point of failure. Two sharing a virtual IP address, or a managed load balancer spread across zones, remove it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. After a guest's key card failed at 2 AM, Cas made /health check everything: the reservations database, the payment service and the key-card machine. On Friday at 11:40 PM the payment service went slow for two minutes. Every room failed its health check three times in a row, so the Doorman took all four out, and for nearly two minutes the website answered 503 to everyone, even guests who only wanted to look at photos of the rooms. All four rooms were running fine the whole time.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What went wrong, and how should /health be written?

keyIdeas.idea: One shared dependency failed every room's check at once, so all four were taken out together
Keep /health shallow: test the server itself, not everything it depends on
Watch dependencies separately, with their own alerts, and let only the pages that need them fail

coldCase.model: The rooms didn't fail; the payment service did, and every room's health check depended on it, so all four failed their checks together and the Doorman took the whole hotel out. A health check should answer one question: should this server get requests? Keep /health shallow: the program is running and can answer. Watch the database and the payment service with their own monitoring and alerts, and let the pages that need payment fail on their own, quickly, while room photos keep working. Some load balancers, like AWS's Application Load Balancer, fail open when every target fails at once and send traffic to all of them on the bet that the checks are wrong. The Doorman doesn't, so Cas should know which kind he has.

Elastic Load Balancing: What is a Network Load Balancer? (functions at the fourth layer of the OSI model; millions of requests per second; flow hash target selection; each TCP connection routed to a single target for its life)
